emt-trauma-l01.q: A child who is 4 feet tall fell from a height. At what fall distance does the mechanism become significant for this child?
choices: More than 10 feet, or about 8 to 12 feet using the 2 to 3 times height rule
emt-trauma-l01.why: Pediatric criteria are more than 10 feet, or 2 to 3 times the child's height, which for a 4-foot child is 8 to 12 feet. The 20-foot figure is the adult threshold and would badly under-triage a child.

emt-trauma-l01.q: A restrained driver has a bruise running diagonally across the abdomen and lower chest. This seat-belt sign should raise suspicion for:
choices: Skin injury only, since the belt did its job
Bowel injury, mesenteric tear or lumbar spine fracture
emt-trauma-l01.why: A belt that leaves a mark transmitted enough force to fold the body at the waist, which ruptures bowel, tears mesentery and fractures the lumbar spine. Treating the bruise as proof the belt worked is the error being tested.

emt-trauma-l02.q: A femoral artery is torn. Roughly how long can it take an adult to lose a frequently fatal volume of blood?
emt-trauma-l02.why: A torn femoral artery can move about 2 liters in two to three minutes, and 2 liters is frequently fatal. That speed is the entire reason exsanguinating hemorrhage is placed before airway in X-A-B-C.

emt-trauma-l02.q: Which technique is NO LONGER part of bleeding control?
choices: Elevation of the limb and pressure points
emt-trauma-l02.why: Elevation and pressure points were dropped because they cost time and were never shown to work. The ladder is direct pressure, tourniquet, packing, then a pressure dressing.

emt-trauma-l03.q: An adult has lost about 1,200 mL of blood. Which class of hemorrhage is this, and what blood pressure do you expect?
choices: Class II, normal blood pressure with a narrowed pulse pressure
Class IV, very low blood pressure
emt-trauma-l03.why: 750 to 1,500 mL is class II: pulse 100-120, an anxious patient, and a blood pressure that is still normal but with a narrowing pulse pressure. The systolic does not fall until class III, around 30 percent loss.

emt-trauma-l03.q: Why is raising the legs no longer recommended for an adult trauma patient in hemorrhagic shock?
choices: It has no proven benefit, and supine positioning is the current recommendation
emt-trauma-l03.why: The shock position was abandoned because studies never showed benefit. Supine is the current recommendation, and the interventions that actually matter are stopping the bleeding, oxygen, warmth and rapid transport.

emt-trauma-l04.q: A patient opens his eyes to your voice, is confused about the date but converses, and withdraws his arm from a pinch. What is his GCS?
emt-trauma-l04.why: Eyes to speech is 3, confused conversation is 4, withdrawal from pain is 4. That totals 11. Localizing pain would be 5 for motor and give 12; obeying commands would be 6 and give 13.

emt-trauma-l04.q: Which single episode roughly DOUBLES mortality in a head-injured patient?
choices: One episode of an SpO2 under 90% or a systolic under 90
A GCS drop of one point
emt-trauma-l04.why: A single hypoxic or hypotensive episode roughly doubles mortality, which is why oxygen and blood pressure are the two treatments for a brain injury. Vomiting and agitation are warning signs, not the mechanism of secondary injury.

emt-trauma-l05.q: How long can a rigid long board begin causing pressure sores?
choices: Long boards do not cause pressure injuries
emt-trauma-l05.why: Pressure sores begin within about 30 minutes, and boards also increase pain and restrict breathing without improving outcomes. That is why the board is now treated as a transfer device, with a vacuum mattress or scoop preferred.

emt-trauma-l05.q: A cervical collar that is sized TOO TALL causes which specific harm?
choices: It extends the neck and can raise intracranial pressure
emt-trauma-l05.why: An oversized collar forces the chin up, extending the neck and raising intracranial pressure. Too short simply does nothing. The collar is measured from the top of the shoulder to the bottom of the chin and never forced.

emt-trauma-l06.q: A chest trauma patient has absent breath sounds on the left with DULL percussion and FLAT neck veins. This best fits:
emt-trauma-l06.why: Blood, not air, fills the space: percussion is dull rather than hyperresonant, and the neck veins are flat because the patient is hypovolemic. Tension gives hyperresonance and distended neck veins; tamponade leaves breath sounds present.

emt-trauma-l06.q: A 14-year-old is struck in the chest by a baseball and collapses pulseless. The most important immediate action is:
choices: Apply a chest seal to the impact site
Begin CPR and get the AED on without delay
emt-trauma-l06.why: This is commotio cordis: a blow in a 10 to 30 millisecond window throws a structurally normal heart into ventricular fibrillation. Because the heart is normal, immediate CPR and early defibrillation work well. Nothing else comes first.

emt-trauma-l07.q: In what order should you palpate the four abdominal quadrants?
choices: Start with the painful quadrant to confirm it
Save the painful quadrant for last
Palpate deeply in all four repeatedly
emt-trauma-l07.why: Palpating the painful quadrant first causes guarding that ruins the rest of the exam. Palpate gently, save the painful quadrant for last, and do not repeatedly re-palpate. You are confirming tenderness, not diagnosing.

emt-trauma-l07.q: An amputated finger is being transported with the patient. Which preparation is correct?
choices: Place it directly on ice in a cup
Wrap in moist sterile gauze, seal in a plastic bag, then place that bag on ice or in cool water
Submerge it in saline and freeze
Wrap it in dry gauze and keep it at room temperature
emt-trauma-l07.why: Moist gauze, sealed bag, then cooled from the outside. Direct contact with ice or freezing destroys the tissue and ends any chance of reattachment. Dry room-temperature storage lets the tissue dry out.

emt-trauma-l08.q: Which of these makes a traction splint CONTRAINDICATED on a femur fracture?
choices: The fracture is in the midshaft
There is a suspected pelvic fracture on the same side
emt-trauma-l08.why: Traction pulls the pelvic ring apart, so a pelvic fracture rules the device out, as do hip or knee injury on the same leg, fractures near the knee, lower leg or ankle fractures, and partial amputations. Midshaft location and a present pulse are what make it appropriate.

emt-trauma-l08.q: A patient with suspected compartment syndrome asks whether to elevate the leg. The correct positioning is:
choices: Elevate well above the heart to reduce swelling
Keep the limb at heart level, because elevation lowers perfusion pressure
emt-trauma-l08.why: Elevation reduces the arterial pressure driving blood into a compartment that is already choking itself, so the limb is kept at heart level. Loosen anything constricting and transport; the pulse stays present until very late and does not rule it out.

emt-trauma-l09.q: A patient has scattered burns over the chest and arms. You estimate them using the patient's palm. Each palm equals about:
emt-trauma-l09.why: The patient's own palm including the fingers is about 1 percent of their body surface, which is why it works for scattered or irregular burns. The 9 percent figure is a whole arm under the rule of nines.

emt-trauma-l09.q: A patient has full-thickness burns to 25% of body surface. Should you cool the burn with water?
choices: No, cooling is only for burns under about 10% and would drop this patient's core temperature
emt-trauma-l09.why: Cooling is limited to small burns under about 10 percent, for 1 to 2 minutes. Cooling a large burn causes hypothermia in a patient who has already lost the skin that holds heat in. Ice is never used on any burn.

emt-trauma-l10.q: Which field triage PHYSIOLOGIC criterion sends a patient to the highest level of trauma care available?
emt-trauma-l10.why: Physiologic criteria come first: GCS 13 or less, systolic under 90, respiratory rate under 10 or over 29. Age, anticoagulants and mechanism are later steps that generally mean a trauma center, not necessarily the highest level.

emt-trauma-l10.q: When does air medical transport genuinely earn its place?
choices: On any trauma call with a significant mechanism
When it saves real time or brings a capability you lack, such as long ground transport or prolonged entrapment
In dense urban areas, where it always beats ground
emt-trauma-l10.why: Helicopters earn their place with long ground transports, prolonged entrapment or inaccessible scenes. In a dense area a helicopter rarely beats the ground unit door to door once you count setup and landing zone time.

emt-trauma-l11.q: A 20 kg child has a total blood volume of roughly how much, and why does that number matter?
choices: About 1.5 L, so a scalp laceration can cause class II hemorrhage
About 3 L, so bleeding is well tolerated
About 5 L, the same as an adult
About 500 mL, so any bleeding is immediately fatal
emt-trauma-l11.why: Blood volume is 70 to 80 mL/kg, so 20 kg is roughly 1.5 liters. A volume of bleeding that is a nuisance in an adult is a substantial fraction of a child's total, and infants can go into shock from a scalp hematoma alone.

emt-trauma-l11.q: The pediatric assessment triangle is read from the doorway and consists of:
choices: Heart rate, blood pressure and respiratory rate
Appearance, work of breathing, and circulation to skin
emt-trauma-l11.why: Appearance, work of breathing and circulation to skin are assessed before you touch the child. A child who will not look at you, will not cry, or does not fight your exam is sick until proven otherwise, regardless of numbers.

emt-trauma-l12.q: Why does a subdural hematoma occur after trivial mechanisms in older patients?
choices: The skull thins with age and fractures easily
Brain shrinkage stretches the bridging veins and leaves space for blood to collect before pressure signs appear
Older patients have higher blood pressure
emt-trauma-l12.why: An atrophied brain puts bridging veins under stretch and creates room for a sizeable collection before any pressure sign shows, which is why these patients can have a normal exam and deteriorate days later.

emt-trauma-l12.q: An 82-year-old on rivaroxaban struck her head and has a completely normal neurologic exam. She should:
choices: Be released with head injury instructions
Receive imaging and usually a period of observation, because the bleed can be delayed by hours
Be transported only if she develops a headache
Be treated the same as a non-anticoagulated patient
emt-trauma-l12.why: Any head strike on an anticoagulant or antiplatelet earns imaging and usually observation, even with a normal exam, because the bleed can declare itself hours later. The field triage guideline treats anticoagulant use with head injury as a trauma center consideration.

emt-trauma-l13.q: You palpate the fundus about 8 cm above the pubic symphysis. Approximately how many weeks pregnant is she?
emt-trauma-l13.why: The fundus reaches the symphysis at about 12 weeks and the umbilicus at about 20, rising roughly 1 cm per week after the symphysis. Eight centimeters above the symphysis is around 20 weeks, which is exactly where left tilt and the pregnancy triage criterion begin.

emt-trauma-l13.q: During CPR on a pregnant patient past 20 weeks, which modification is required?
choices: Continuous manual left uterine displacement, with standard hand placement on the sternum
emt-trauma-l13.why: Manual left displacement keeps the uterus off the vena cava while leaving the chest flat for effective compressions; hand placement stays standard on the lower half of the sternum, since moving the hands higher is no longer recommended. Tilting the board compromises compression quality, and depth is never reduced.

emt-trauma-l14.q: Why does the diaphragm make a wound at the nipple line an abdominal injury too?
choices: The diaphragm sits permanently at the nipple line
The diaphragm rises as high as the fourth intercostal space on a full exhalation
Abdominal organs extend into the chest normally
The nipple line marks the bottom of the lung
emt-trauma-l14.why: On full exhalation the diaphragm climbs to about the fourth intercostal space, so anything entering the thoracoabdominal zone may have crossed into the belly. That is why a stab below the nipple is treated as both a chest and an abdominal injury.

emt-trauma-l14.q: Which dressing is correct for an open wound on the side of the neck, and why?
choices: A circumferential wrap for even pressure
An occlusive dressing with direct pressure over the vessel, never wrapped around the neck
Dry gauze taped on three sides
emt-trauma-l14.why: An occlusive dressing prevents air being sucked into an injured vein, which causes air embolism. Pressure goes over the vessel only; wrapping circumferentially, or dressing both sides at once, obstructs the airway and the opposite carotid.

emt-trauma-l15.q: A crushed limb can third-space roughly how much fluid over 48 hours?
choices: Fluid shift does not occur in crush injury
emt-trauma-l15.why: A badly crushed limb can sequester 10 to 12 liters over 48 hours, which means the patient is already hypovolemic before anything is lifted. That is part of why fluid is started before release, not after.

emt-trauma-l15.q: Why is an enclosed-space explosion more dangerous than the same device detonated outdoors?
choices: The pressure wave reflects off surfaces instead of dissipating, multiplying the overpressure
emt-trauma-l15.why: Reflection off walls multiplies overpressure, so the same device that bruises someone in a parking lot kills someone on a bus. Underwater blasts do the same thing. Smoke and access matter but are not the physics being tested.

emt-trauma-l16.q: Why is a belt or electrical cord a poor improvised tourniquet?
choices: It is too wide to tighten
It is too narrow to occlude arterial flow but can still obstruct venous return, which worsens bleeding
emt-trauma-l16.why: A strap should be at least 1.5 inches wide to spread pressure. Narrow improvised materials are hard to tension, often fail to stop arterial inflow, and still block venous outflow, so the limb bleeds more than before.

emt-trauma-l16.q: Which is NOT a criterion for tourniquet conversion?
choices: Less than about 2 hours since application
The patient is not in shock
The patient reports significant pain from the device
You can observe the wound continuously and retighten
emt-trauma-l16.why: Pain is explicitly not a conversion criterion. Conversion requires a short elapsed time, no shock, plausibly controllable bleeding, no amputation or mangled limb, continuous observation, and a transport long enough for the limb to benefit.

emt-trauma-l17.q: Roughly what proportion of pelvic bleeding is venous and from broken bone surfaces?
choices: Almost none; it is nearly all arterial
emt-trauma-l17.why: 80 to 90 percent is venous and from bone surfaces, which is why closing the ring works at all: venous bleeding stops when the space stops expanding and pressure can build enough to tamponade.

emt-trauma-l17.q: After tightening a binder, which additional step further closes the pelvic ring?
choices: Rotating the feet slightly inward and tying the knees and ankles together
Log-rolling the patient onto the injured side
emt-trauma-l17.why: Internal rotation of the legs closes the ring further, so the feet are turned slightly inward and the knees and ankles tied with cravats or wide tape. Elevation, further rolling and hip flexion all move the unstable ring rather than closing it.

emt-trauma-l18.q: About how long does muscle tolerate complete ischemia before it dies?
emt-trauma-l18.why: Roughly 4 to 6 hours, which is why a pulseless angulated limb earns one gentle realignment attempt and why a persistently pulseless extremity is announced on the radio; it changes the receiving team's plan.

emt-trauma-l18.q: Which dislocation is the one most feared because of the artery tethered behind it?
choices: Knee dislocation and the popliteal artery
Posterior hip dislocation and the femoral artery
emt-trauma-l18.why: The popliteal artery is tethered behind the knee and is injured in a large minority of true knee dislocations, even ones that appear to relocate themselves. Posterior hip dislocation threatens the sciatic NERVE, not the femoral artery.

emt-trauma-l19.q: What is the preferred FIRST equipment step for a football player with a suspected spine injury who needs airway access?
choices: Remove the face mask, leaving the helmet and pads in place
Remove both helmet and pads together
emt-trauma-l19.why: Removing the face mask frees the entire airway while the helmet and its padding hold the head where it is. Removing the helmet alone extends the neck, and removing pads alone flexes it; they come off together or not at all.

emt-trauma-l19.q: An unresponsive athlete is found prone. The correct way to turn him is:
choices: Roll him quickly by the shoulders
Turn him supine as a unit, with the provider at the head starting with crossed arms so their hands unwind into position
Leave him prone and ventilate through the face mask
Lift him straight up and flip him
emt-trauma-l19.why: The crossed-arm start lets the head provider maintain control through the entire roll as their hands unwind. Rolling by the shoulders moves the spine independently, and leaving an unresponsive athlete prone gives you no airway control.

quiz.q: A car travelling 20 mph and an identical car travelling 60 mph both strike a pole. Approximately how much more kinetic energy does the faster crash deliver?
quiz.why: Kinetic energy rises with the square of speed, and tripling speed multiplies energy by nine. Answers that scale linearly with speed are the trap, and they are why speed is the first question you ask about a crash.

quiz.q: Which type of penetrating trauma damages tissue several inches off the wound track?
choices: A high-velocity rifle wound, through cavitation
quiz.why: High-velocity projectiles drag a pressure wave that stretches and tears tissue well off the path, an effect called cavitation. Knives and ice picks injure only what the blade touched, and a handgun sits between the two.

quiz.q: You arrive at a crash where the airbag has deployed and the driver says the bag caught him. What should you do before accepting that?
choices: Nothing; a deployed airbag means the chest was protected
Lift the deflated bag and inspect the steering wheel for deformity
Measure the distance from the seat to the wheel
quiz.why: Airbags deploy and deflate in about 0.05 seconds, so by the time you arrive the bag is limp and tells you nothing. A deformed steering wheel under it means the chest hit hard regardless of what the patient says.

quiz.q: You are holding direct pressure on a bleeding forearm laceration. How long should you hold before checking?
choices: Until the patient says it has stopped
quiz.why: A full 3 minutes without lifting the dressing lets a clot form. Peeking early pulls the forming clot off. If the dressing soaks through, add more on top and never remove the first one.

quiz.q: A tourniquet is needed for a wound just below the left knee. Where do you place it?
choices: On the thigh, above the knee joint
As close to the wound as possible
quiz.why: A tourniquet never goes over a joint, so a wound at or just below the knee means going above the knee onto the thigh. Placing it below the wound does nothing, and crossing the joint prevents the device from compressing the artery.

quiz.q: A patient has a severe nosebleed after being punched. There is no suspicion of skull fracture. The correct position is:
choices: Sitting up, leaning forward, pinching the soft part of the nose for 10 to 15 minutes
Sitting up, head tilted back, pinching the bridge
Sitting up with the nose packed with gauze
quiz.why: Leaning forward keeps blood out of the throat, which prevents vomiting and airway compromise. Pinching is on the soft part, not the bony bridge, and is held without releasing to check. Packing is never done after head trauma with suspected skull fracture.

quiz.q: Which set of findings best describes compensated shock in an adult?
choices: Systolic of 70, unresponsive, weak thready pulse
Normal blood pressure, heart rate 118, pale cool clammy skin, capillary refill 3 seconds, anxious
Warm dry pink skin, heart rate 52, systolic 84
Normal vital signs with no complaints
quiz.why: Compensated shock is the adrenaline picture with a blood pressure that has not yet fallen. A low systolic with altered mental status is decompensated. Warm dry skin with bradycardia and hypotension is the neurogenic pattern, not hemorrhagic.

quiz.q: Which leg of the lethal triad is most directly under an EMT's control?
quiz.why: Cutting away wet clothing, blanketing the patient and heating the compartment directly prevent hypothermia, and cold blood does not clot. Acidosis and coagulopathy are downstream consequences that an EMT influences only indirectly through warmth and hemorrhage control.

quiz.q: Why is a hypotensive child treated as a near-arrest?
choices: Children have smaller hearts and tire quickly
A child's vessels clamp down ferociously and hold a normal pressure until nearly exsanguinated, then crash without warning
Pediatric blood pressure cuffs are unreliable
quiz.why: Children compensate harder and longer than adults, so hypotension means the compensation has already failed and a very large fraction of blood volume is gone. Children generate marked tachycardia, which is why heart rate, skin and mental status are the signs you watch.

quiz.q: Which GCS verbal score corresponds to a patient who makes only incomprehensible groaning sounds?
quiz.why: Verbal scoring is 5 oriented, 4 confused conversation, 3 inappropriate words, 2 incomprehensible sounds, 1 none. Groaning with no words is a 2. Scoring it as 1 would only apply if there were no sound at all.

quiz.q: An elderly heavy drinker fell two weeks ago and now has a gradually worsening headache and confusion. Which injury does this pattern fit?
quiz.why: Subdural bleeding is venous and slow, from stretched bridging veins, and is common in the elderly and heavy drinkers whose brains have shrunk. Epidurals are arterial and fast with a lucid interval. Concussion improves rather than worsens over two weeks.

quiz.q: A 5-year-old struck his head, has a GCS of 15 and a normal exam, but vomited once. The correct action is:
choices: Release to the parents with instructions
Transport, because vomiting even once after a head injury is a red flag, especially in a child
Transport only if he vomits a second time
quiz.why: A single episode of vomiting after a head injury earns transport, and that is emphasized in children. Waiting for a second episode or observing on scene both delay identification of a bleed that has not yet produced any other sign.

quiz.q: Which mechanism most directly threatens the cervical spine through axial loading?
choices: A fall onto an outstretched hand
quiz.why: Axial loading drives force straight down the spine, which is what a headfirst dive, a head-down tackle or a landing on the head or feet do. Low-speed rear-end impacts produce flexion and extension, and a fall onto a hand loads the wrist.

quiz.q: A patient with penetrating trauma to the torso has no neurologic deficit. Spinal motion restriction is:
choices: Generally not indicated, because it delays surgery without benefit
Indicated only if the wound is above the nipple line
Indicated for gunshot wounds but not stab wounds
quiz.why: Restriction for isolated penetrating trauma without a deficit delays definitive surgery and is associated with worse outcomes. If a neurologic deficit is present, restrict. Wound location and weapon type do not change the rule.

quiz.q: A stable, alert, cooperative patient is still seated in a vehicle with plenty of time available. The technique producing the least spinal movement is:
choices: A collar and self-extrication, with the patient turning, standing and pivoting to the stretcher
A long board slid under the patient from the side
quiz.why: Self-extrication by a cooperative patient produces measurably less spinal motion than any provider-performed technique. Rapid extrication is for the unstable patient. A vest device remains an option where protocol calls for it, but it moves the spine more.

quiz.q: A tension pneumothorax kills primarily by:
choices: Preventing oxygen exchange in the collapsed lung
Pushing the mediastinum across and kinking the great veins, which drops cardiac output
quiz.why: It is a circulation problem: mediastinal shift kinks the veins returning blood to the heart. The lung collapse contributes but is not what kills. Tracheal deviation is a late external sign of the shift, not an airway obstruction.

quiz.q: Why is taping or sandbagging a flail segment wrong?
choices: It is uncomfortable for the patient
It restricts chest wall movement and worsens ventilation; positive-pressure ventilation splints the segment from the inside instead
It hides the injury from the trauma team
It causes rib displacement into the lung
quiz.why: External binding restricts the whole chest wall, not just the flail, and worsens ventilation in a patient whose real problem is the pulmonary contusion underneath. Positive pressure by bag-valve mask or CPAP per protocol splints from the inside.

quiz.q: Fractures of ribs 9 through 12 on the LEFT should raise suspicion for injury to which organ?
quiz.why: The spleen sits under the lower left ribs and the liver under the lower right, so side determines the organ. Ribs 1 and 2 fractured anywhere mean enormous force was applied.

quiz.q: Which abdominal injury pattern typically looks mild at the scene and becomes catastrophic over hours?
quiz.why: Hollow organs spill acid, bile and stool, and the resulting chemical and then bacterial peritonitis builds over hours. Solid organs announce themselves earlier by bleeding, and superficial injuries do not deteriorate.

quiz.q: A patient has an evisceration of small bowel through an abdominal wound. Which positioning is correct?
choices: Supine with the knees flexed to take tension off the abdominal wall
quiz.why: Flexed knees relax the abdominal wall so the wound is under less tension. Straight legs and sitting both stretch the abdomen, and prone positioning crushes the exposed bowel. Cover with moist sterile then occlusive dressing and never replace the organs.

quiz.q: A patient has a large flap of skin torn loose on the forearm, still attached at one edge. Correct care is:
choices: Cut the flap off and dress the wound
Clean gross debris, lay the flap back into its anatomic position, then dress
Fold the flap back and tape it open
Pack the wound under the flap with hemostatic gauze
quiz.why: An avulsion flap is returned to its anatomic position after gross debris is removed, because the flap may survive. Cutting it off removes tissue the surgeon may need, and tissue torn completely free travels with the patient.

quiz.q: Approximately how much blood can a closed femur fracture hide in the thigh?
quiz.why: A closed femur can hide 1 to 1.5 liters, enough to produce class II or III hemorrhage with no external blood at all. A pelvic fracture can hide 2 liters or more, which is why unexplained shock points at the belly, pelvis or femurs.

quiz.q: Which splint is best suited to a clavicle fracture?
choices: Rigid board splint from shoulder to wrist
quiz.why: The sling carries the weight and the swathe binds the arm to the chest so it cannot swing, which is what a clavicle, shoulder or most humerus injuries need. Traction splints are only for isolated closed midshaft femurs, and air splints are for the lower leg and forearm.

quiz.q: Which splint type has the disadvantage that its internal pressure shifts with temperature and altitude?
quiz.why: Air splints gain or lose pressure as temperature or altitude changes, so a splint that was snug can become a tourniquet or fall loose. A vacuum splint conforms to angulated limbs and does not have that problem.

quiz.q: A 3-year-old weighing 15 kg has burns to the entire head and the entire left leg. Using pediatric proportions, the approximate burn surface area is:
quiz.why: In a small child the head is 18 percent and each leg is 13.5 percent, totaling 31.5 percent. Using adult proportions of 9 and 18 would give 27 percent and significantly under-estimate the burn in a child.

quiz.q: A full-thickness burn is described by the patient as painless in the center. This should be interpreted as:
choices: Reassuring, because the patient is comfortable
Ominous, because the nerve endings have been destroyed
Evidence the burn is only superficial
A sign of adequate pain medication
quiz.why: Painless means the nerve endings are dead, which is a marker of depth, not of a mild injury. Partial thickness burns are intensely painful precisely because the nerves are still alive and exposed.

quiz.q: An electrical burn patient has a small wound on the hand and another on the foot. What should you anticipate?
choices: Only local tissue injury at the two wounds
A path of cooked tissue between them, plus dysrhythmias, fractures and possible spinal injury from tetanic contraction
Rapid healing since the wounds are small
quiz.why: The entry and exit wounds are the ends of an unseen path of damaged tissue. Expect cardiac dysrhythmias requiring monitoring and an AED available, and expect fractures, dislocations and spinal injury from violent muscle contraction.

quiz.q: A patient has a chemical splash of a dry powder on the skin. The correct first step is:
choices: Brush the dry powder off first, then flush
Neutralize the agent with a base
Cover with a dry dressing and transport
quiz.why: Water activates dry lime and similar agents, so the powder is brushed off before flushing. Then flush with copious water for at least 20 minutes, continuing during transport. Neutralizing an acid with a base generates heat and makes the burn worse.

quiz.q: Which eye injury care principle is correct?
choices: Cover only the injured eye so the patient can still see
Cover both eyes, because the uninjured eye tracks and the injured one follows
Remove contact lenses in all eye injuries
Apply firm pressure to a suspected ruptured globe to stop bleeding
quiz.why: Covering both eyes stops consensual movement of the injured eye. Contacts come out only for chemical burns, and pressure on a suspected ruptured globe extrudes its contents. An impaled object in the eye is stabilized with a rigid cup taped over it.

quiz.q: Which trauma center level has full surgical subspecialty coverage 24/7 plus research and residency requirements?
quiz.why: Level I is the highest capability, with round-the-clock subspecialty coverage plus research and residency. Level II has 24/7 surgery without the research requirement, Level III stabilizes and transfers complex cases, and Level IV may have no surgeon at all.

quiz.q: What is the platinum ten, and why does it matter more than the golden hour?
choices: Ten minutes of CPR before transport; it improves ROSC
A scene time target of 10 minutes; scene time is the delay an EMT actually controls
Ten minutes of oxygen before moving a trauma patient
Ten minutes of direct pressure on any wound
quiz.why: The golden hour is a slogan rather than data, but bleeding patients do worse with delay and scene time is the delay you control. Load and go, and do the rest en route.

quiz.q: A 2-year-old fell and has a heart rate of 178 with a blood pressure of 88/52 and capillary refill of 4 seconds. Your partner says the pressure is normal so the child is stable. The correct response is:
choices: Explain that tachycardia with delayed capillary refill is compensated shock, and a child's normal pressure means nothing yet
Repeat the blood pressure in the other arm before deciding
Attribute the heart rate to crying
quiz.why: Children hold blood pressure until they cannot, then crash without a warning slide. Tachycardia is the earliest reliable sign of pediatric shock, and delayed capillary refill confirms it. Waiting to reassess is never the answer to this stem.

quiz.q: Why can a child have a severe pulmonary contusion with no rib fractures?
choices: Pediatric ribs are partly cartilage and bend rather than break, transmitting force to the lung underneath
Children's lungs are more resistant to injury
Rib fractures in children heal before you arrive
quiz.why: Flexible ribs absorb and transmit energy without fracturing, so the chest wall looks perfectly normal over a badly bruised lung. The reverse is also informative: rib fractures in a small child mean enormous force was applied.

quiz.q: Which finding in a 9-month-old most strongly raises concern for inflicted injury?
choices: Bruising on the ears and neck in a child who is not yet cruising
A small scalp abrasion after a witnessed fall
quiz.why: Bruising on the torso, ears or neck of a child under 4, and any bruise on an infant who is not yet crawling or cruising, are red flags, as are patterned burns, changing stories and infant rib fractures. Shin bruises are ordinary in mobile children. NJ EMTs are mandatory reporters.

quiz.q: A 70-year-old has three fractured ribs after a ground-level fall. Why is this a trauma-center problem?
choices: Rib fractures in the elderly always puncture the lung
Pain produces shallow breathing, which collapses alveoli and invites pneumonia, and mortality rises with each additional fractured rib after 65
Elderly ribs cannot heal without surgery
quiz.why: Each additional fractured rib in a patient over 65 raises mortality and pneumonia risk through the pain-shallow breathing-atelectasis pathway. Three or more in an older adult is a trauma-center problem even without an obvious lung injury.

quiz.q: Which reversal agent is matched correctly to its drug?
quiz.why: Idarucizumab reverses dabigatran. Warfarin is reversed with vitamin K plus factor concentrate, factor Xa inhibitors like apixaban and rivaroxaban with andexanet alfa or factor concentrate, and antiplatelets such as clopidogrel have no true reversal agent.

quiz.q: Why is fragile elderly skin a practical problem in trauma care?
choices: It tears under tape, so roller gauze and soft dressings are preferred
quiz.why: Paper-thin skin tears when taped and then removed, creating a new wound. Roller gauze and soft dressings hold the same dressings without that damage. Older patients also lose heat quickly and should be warmed early.

quiz.q: Placental abruption is best described as:
choices: A tear in the uterine wall itself
The placenta shearing off the uterine wall, the leading cause of fetal death when the mother survives
quiz.why: Abruption is a shearing separation caused by deceleration, so it follows crashes and falls that look survivable. Its bleeding is often concealed behind the placenta and it can declare itself hours later. Uterine rupture is a different, rarer and more catastrophic injury.

quiz.q: Where should a pregnant patient's lap belt sit?
choices: Across the top of the uterus
Low across the hips and under the belly
Across the middle of the abdomen
Over the shoulder only, with no lap belt
quiz.why: The lap belt goes low across the hips and under the belly, with the shoulder belt between the breasts and off to the side of the uterus. A belt riding across the uterus transmits force straight into the placenta. Airbags are not contraindicated in pregnancy.

quiz.q: Why must you ask a pregnant trauma patient her blood type?
choices: An Rh-negative mother needs Rh immune globulin after even minor abdominal trauma
It predicts the risk of abruption
It determines the fetal heart rate target
quiz.why: Rh-negative mothers require Rh immune globulin after abdominal trauma, even minor, to prevent sensitization. Blood type does not predict abruption or determine destination, and fetal heart targets are not set by maternal blood type.

quiz.q: Which neck zone runs from the cricoid cartilage to the angle of the jaw and is the most commonly injured?
quiz.why: Zone II is the most exposed and most commonly injured. Zone I runs from the clavicles to the cricoid and contains the great vessels and the top of the chest; Zone III runs above the jaw angle to the skull base and is difficult to reach surgically. There is no Zone IV.

quiz.q: Why should you never probe or irrigate a penetrating wound to trace its path?
choices: It is painful for the patient
It restarts bleeding that had stopped and teaches you nothing the operating room will not learn better
It is outside the EMT scope of practice
quiz.why: Probing disrupts clot and can start bleeding that had tamponaded, with no diagnostic gain. Count holes and expose fully instead, including the back, axilla, groin and scalp, because an odd number of holes means something is still inside.

quiz.q: Which detail will the trauma team specifically ask you for after a shooting, and which you must gather at the scene?
choices: The weapon type, number of shots heard, and distance from the shooter
The responding police officer's badge number
quiz.why: Weapon type and caliber, shots heard, distance and, for stabbings, blade length and angle, all shape the surgical plan. Bystanders and police who know these facts will be gone in ten minutes, which is why it is gathered at the scene.

quiz.q: Which laboratory-visible consequence of crush syndrome causes the urine to turn tea-colored and injures the kidneys?
quiz.why: Myoglobin clogs the kidney tubules and turns the urine tea or cola colored. Hyperkalemia is the finding that kills fastest by stopping the heart, hypocalcemia develops as calcium is dragged into damaged muscle, and lactic acid worsens rhythm and clotting problems.

quiz.q: At roughly what overpressure do eardrums rupture, and what does a ruptured eardrum tell you about blast lung?
choices: 5 psi, and it reliably predicts blast lung
5 psi, and it is not a reliable screen for blast lung
15 psi, and it rules out blast lung
40 psi, and it confirms blast lung
quiz.why: Eardrums rupture around 5 psi and lung injury generally needs 15 to 40 psi, but plenty of patients have one without the other in each direction. Using intact eardrums to clear a blast patient's lungs is the error being tested.

quiz.q: Why do responders avoid clustering and avoid the obvious approach lane at a bombing?
choices: To keep the scene photogenic for investigators
Because secondary devices are timed and placed for responders
quiz.why: Secondary devices target the people who come to help, so do not park in the obvious approach lane, do not cluster, do not touch unattended bags, and move patients away from the structure before working on them.

quiz.q: Which statement about tourniquet safe time reflects current evidence?
choices: Routine safe time is about 2 hours and limbs have been salvaged after 6 hours
A tourniquet must be removed within 1 hour or amputation is certain
Time does not matter at all
quiz.why: Routine safe time is about 2 hours, and salvage has occurred out to 6 hours on a properly applied device. Limb loss from the tourniquet itself is rare; the wound that made you reach for it is the real threat to the limb.

quiz.q: During a conversion attempt, you loosen the windlass and bleeding restarts. You should:
choices: Retighten the device and do not attempt conversion again
Remove the tourniquet and pack the wound harder
Leave it loose and apply a pressure dressing
quiz.why: One failed attempt ends the attempt. Retighten and leave it. The technique is to pack and dress first, loosen slowly without removing the device, watch a full 2 minutes, and keep the loosened device in place ready to retighten.

quiz.q: Tranexamic acid works by:
choices: Creating new clot at the bleeding site
Occupying the plasminogen binding site on fibrin so existing clot is not dissolved prematurely
quiz.why: TXA is an antifibrinolytic: it protects the clot you or the body already made rather than creating clot. That is why it never replaces pressure, packing or a tourniquet, and why it is given within the 3-hour window after injury.

quiz.q: A pelvis broken in one obvious place should make you suspect:
choices: An isolated injury that will heal without surgery
A second break elsewhere in the ring, because a ring cannot break in only one place
A hip dislocation on the same side
quiz.why: A ring must break in at least two places to deform, so one obvious fracture implies another injury on the opposite side. That is also why closing the whole ring with a binder, rather than splinting one fracture, is the treatment.

quiz.q: Before applying a pelvic binder, why must you empty the pockets and cut away clothing?
choices: Because a phone, wallet or keys trapped under the binder produces a pressure ulcer within about an hour
To allow the binder to adhere to the skin
quiz.why: Any hard object under a tensioned binder concentrates pressure and ulcerates skin within about an hour. Binders do not adhere to skin, and the point is injury prevention, not searching the patient.

quiz.q: Which pelvic fracture pattern is the one a binder helps MOST?
quiz.why: The open book pattern springs the front of the ring apart, which is exactly what a binder closes. Lateral compression still benefits but over-tightening can push fragments further in, and vertical shear is highly unstable and less well controlled by a binder.

quiz.q: An open tibia fracture has bone protruding. Correct care of the exposed bone is:
choices: Push it gently back beneath the skin to reduce contamination
Cover it with a moist sterile dressing and do not push it back in
Cover with a dry dressing and apply traction
Leave it uncovered so the surgeon can inspect it
quiz.why: Moist sterile covering prevents the bone end drying out; pushing it back deliberately drags contamination inward. If a justified realignment for a pulseless limb causes the bone to slide under on its own, that is acceptable but must be reported at handoff.

quiz.q: An ankle fracture-dislocation has white, tented, blanched skin over a bone end. Many protocols permit which action here?
choices: Immediate removal of the bone fragment
A gentle field reduction, because that skin will die before the patient reaches an operating room
Elevation above the heart for 20 minutes
quiz.why: Skin about to break over a deformity is one of the two exceptions to splinting as found, the other being a pulseless limb. Follow protocol and contact medical direction. Traction splints are for femurs, not ankles.

quiz.q: How should an injured hand be positioned for splinting?
choices: In the position of function, a slight cup achieved with a roll of gauze in the palm
quiz.why: The position of function preserves the hand's usable geometry while it heals. Rings, watches and bracelets come off at the first opportunity, before swelling turns them into tourniquets, and injured fingers are buddy-taped with padding between.

quiz.q: A wrestler has burning pain and weakness down ONE arm after a hit, resolving within two minutes. This is best described as:
choices: Transient quadriplegia requiring immobilization and transport
A stinger, a brachial plexus stretch, which still warrants examination
Normal post-contact soreness requiring no assessment
quiz.why: One arm affected and resolving quickly is a brachial plexus stretch, not a cord injury, though the athlete is still examined. Symptoms in ALL FOUR limbs after axial loading are transient quadriplegia, and that athlete is immobilized and transported even if they feel fine.
